This article investigates the Data and Power Integrated Transfer (DPIT) technique, a new approach that surpasses the benefits of multiple antennas and carriers. We derive exact expressions for the output signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of SISO-OFDM, MISO-OFDM, and the optimal power allocation strategy for DPIT. Additionally, we derive the capacity-approaching boundary for DPIT. Analyzing the maximum average output SNR (MAOSNR) metrics for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM, we observe that the topological configuration significantly impacts performance. We further analyze the impact of bandwidth and wavelength effects on DPIT. Numerical results demonstrate that the MAOSNR is not always directly proportional to the average input SNR for MISO-OFDM and SISO-OFDM. We also analyze the scalar multiple access channel (SMAC) model, concluding that DPIT performs better than multiple-input single-output (MISO) and single-input multiple-output (SIMO) systems when the noiseless signal portions are uncorrelated. Moreover, we observe that the optimal power splitting ratio between data and side information does not depend on the side information's signal-to-noise ratio. Lastly, we analyze the SMAC model's capacity-approaching boundary, observing that the waterfilling pattern may not always optimize the capacity for the general case but does so in the Gaussian case. In the Gaussian case, we derive the capacity-approaching boundary's simplest form. We also analyze the capacity-approaching boundary's average capacity performance for the Rayleigh channel, observing that the capacity approaches the optimal capacity as the signal-to-noise ratio increases. Furthermore, we analyze the capacity-approaching boundary's average capacity performance for the AWGN channel, observing that the capacity approaches the optimal capacity as the signal-to-noise ratio decreases. Lastly, we provide code for the capacity-approaching boundary's numerical evaluation.

In the realm of CPUs, a critical performance factor is the data rate between levels of the pipeline, which directly affects clock rates and, by extension, training times and energy expenditure. In the present study, we explore the design of the CPU's data transfer rates in microprocessors, focusing on the level 2 (L2) to level 3 (L3) interface and its impact on training times and energy consumption. We design and experiment with multiple variations of this interface, incorporating novel ideas such as a split L2 cache and a hybrid memory access scheme. Ultimately, we develop a low-power CPU architecture with significantly reduced data transfer rates, demonstrating the feasibility of slowing down data transfer rates without impairing performance and even sometimes enhancing it. Based on our findings, we created a low-power CPU architecture with an operating frequency of 1.4 times the data transfer frequency, concluding that designing efficient data transfer rates offers a new avenue for improving performance per unit of energy expenditure. Furthermore, we built a low-power CPU architecture with an operating frequency of 1.4 times the data transfer frequency, ending up with a 37% improvement in performance per unit of energy expenditure over the Intel Silverlake architecture and a 25% improvement over the AMD Zen 3 architecture. As a result, designers of microprocessors now have additional design options to consider. Additionally, we made our designs publicly available to facilitate use in the development of custom processors.

This leads to numerous possible reconstructions, which might include unphysical components like negativity. We examine how difficulties in state reconstruction correlate with measures of entanglement and synchronization, analyzing potential challenges associated with identifying non-linear properties and even genuine non-locality. Furthermore, we explore how issues with reconstruction procedures might hinder detecting the onset of quantum synchronization. To address these challenges, we propose an alternative method for extracting the entanglement degree from a tomogram, one that only relies on non-negative data and could be particularly useful for identifying sources of entanglement. This approach is based on a linear map that highlights parts of the Hilbert space accessible through the given data, aligning with the region where the entanglement measure would be computed. This method is applicable universally but is particularly valuable for situations where the reconstructed state includes unphysical components or fails to produce a legitimate description. We apply this proposal to an experiment where two continuously entangled light sources are created, with one of the setups producing an axis that doesn't correspond to any physical state along the reconstructed description. In this latter scenario, the proposed method is capable of determining the entanglement degree correctly, leading to a description of a physical state that includes the genuinely entangled portion. This approach can also be used to define regions of a Hilbert space that are accessible through legitimate state reconstructions for various types of non-linear relationships, suchating the presence of both global and specific types of synchronization. Moreover, this method can help distinguish between different kinds of non-local connections by comparing the areas defined by distinct measures of non-linearity, concluding that the measure of concurrence is more sensitive to the source of entanglement than the measure of entanglement itself.
